catalog_quote: 3.3.1 Stress 3.3.1.1 Phonemic Primary Stress Phonemic primary stress /´/ incorporates high tone. It does not occur word initially in polysyllabic words and no more than one occurrence per word has been observed. It most commonly occurs word finally. Some words have no primary stress. Monosyllabic word patterns: /úk/ ... 'to whimper' /pú/ ... 'canoe paddle' ... /pæ̀/ ... 'bracelet' /ɓò/ ... 'bench' Disyllabic word patterns: /ùlís/ ... 'rope' /sèkáʔ/ ... 'boy' /ìhùn/ ... 'nose' /kàmòt/ ... 'to beckon' ... 3.3.1.2 Non-phonemic Secondary Stress Non-phonemic secondary stress ... incorporates mid tone. It occurs word initially. It can be thought of as an allophone of non-stress ... 3.3.1.3 Phonemic Non-stress Phonemic non-stress ... incorporates mid-tone when following a primary stressed syllable and a low tone elsewhere.

tone_statements.citation: Cahill, Michael. 2011. Tonal diversity in languages of Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-008. Dallas: SIL International. 23 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Some have what may be labeled a pitch-accent system, e.g., Tinputz (Hostetler and Hostetler 1975), with one stress manifested as High tone per word (though some words lack this).
tone_statements.summary: pitch accent label: at most one 'stress' per word, realised as High tone; some words have none. Nothing further (no TBU, no tone inventory) is stated for Tinputz.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2009. How (not) to do phonological typology: the case of pitch accent. Language Sciences 31(2-3): 213-238. (Sec. 3.2 'Culminativity', ex. (13): word-tone patterns of Tinputz after Hostetler & Hostetler 1975.)
tone_statements.quote: Turning to culminativity, (13) displays the word-tone patterns of Tinputz [Austronesian; Papua New Guinea] (Hostetler and Hostetler, 1975). ... As seen, all-L words are possible in Tinputz, but CULM(H) restricts words to a single /H/. In addition, words may not begin with a H, unless monosyllabic, which I have analyzed as /LH/. Other languages with culminative, but non-obligatory /H/ include Somali (and several related Cushitic languages), Agiribi Kiwai (Wurm, 1973; Donohue, 1997), Yucatec Mayan (Gussenhoven, 2007), and Ocaina [Witotoan; Peru] (Agnew and Pike, 1957).

sources.quote: Turning to culminativity, (13) displays the word-tone patterns of Tinputz [Austronesian; Papua New Guinea] (Hostetler and Hostetler, 1975). ... As seen, all-L words are possible in Tinputz, but CULM(H) restricts words to a single /H/. In addition, words may not begin with a H, unless monosyllabic, which I have analyzed as /LH/. Other languages with culminative, but non-obligatory /H/ include Somali (and several related Cushitic languages), Agiribi Kiwai (Wurm, 1973; Donohue, 1997), Yucatec Mayan (Gussenhoven, 2007), and Ocaina [Witotoan; Peru] (Agnew and Pike, 1957).
sources.locator: p. 221, Sec. 3.2 'Culminativity (CULM)', example (13); cross-reference p. 223 ('Recall the absence of initial H also in Tinputz in (13)')
sources.note: Reanalyses Hostetler & Hostetler's 'phonemic primary stress incorporating high tone' as a privative /H/ vs. zero tone system in which H is culminative (at most one /H/ per word) but not obligatory (all-L words exist), and word-initial H is barred except in monosyllables (analysed as /LH/); Tinputz is grouped with Somali, Arigibi Kiwai, Yucatec Maya and Ocaina as 'culminative but non-obligatory /H/' languages, i.e. a tonal rather than accentual treatment.
